title: Stop Loss vs Stop Limit Order for Beginners: Avoid Bad Fills
meta_description: Stop loss vs stop limit order for beginners: what each does, a simple gap-down example, trailing stops, Day vs GTC, and the mistakes that cost money.
quick_answer: A stop-loss (stop-market) sell order becomes a market order once the stock trades at or below your stop price. It will very likely sell, but possibly well below your stop if the price gaps or drops fast. A stop-limit order becomes a limit order instead. It never sells below your limit price, but it may not sell at all. You get a likely exit or price control, never both.
key_takeaways: A stop-loss (stop-market) order is very likely to get you out, but it doesn't promise a price. In a fast drop or an overnight gap it can fill well below your stop.
A stop-limit order promises a minimum price, but it doesn't promise an exit. If the stock gaps below your limit, the order may not fill and you still own the shares.
No basic stop order can protect you from a gap. It only decides what happens after the price has already moved.
Trailing stops rise with the price but usually become market orders, so they carry the same gap risk as a stop-loss.
Choose Day or GTC on purpose, keep stops outside the stock's normal daily swings, and review your open orders after every trade or stock split.
Long-term investors in diversified index funds often manage risk with their asset mix and an emergency fund instead of stops.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for new investors who see 'Stop', 'Stop Limit' and 'Trailing Stop' on their broker's sell screen and want to understand what each one does, and what can go wrong, before using it.
intro: When you tap Sell in a brokerage app, you'll usually see a list of order types: Market, Limit, Stop, Stop Limit and Trailing Stop. The last three sound like safety features, and in a way they are. But each one has a weak spot that catches beginners off guard. The biggest surprise comes when a stock gaps down overnight. A stop-loss can sell far below the price you set, and a stop-limit may not sell at all. This guide explains both in plain language and walks through a gap-down example with simple, made-up numbers. It also covers trailing stops, how long an order stays active, common mistakes that cost new investors money, a simple order-log template, and why many long-term index investors don't use stops at all. This is general information, not trading advice. How orders work depends on your broker, and rules and taxes differ by country.

steps.name: Decide what the stop is for
steps.text: Write one sentence explaining why you want a stop, for example to cap the loss on a single stock or to protect a gain. If you can't name a clear reason, you may not need one. Many long-term index investors don't use stops.

steps.name: Check how the stock normally moves
steps.text: Open your broker's chart and look at the stock's usual daily and weekly price range over the past few months. Some platforms also show an average true range (ATR) indicator, which measures typical price movement. A stop set inside that normal range is likely to be triggered by everyday ups and downs.

steps.name: Choose the order type
steps.text: On the sell order screen, pick Stop (stop-loss or stop-market) if getting out matters most. Pick Stop Limit if avoiding a bad price matters most. Pick Trailing Stop if you want the stop to rise as the price rises. Remember that only a stop-market order is likely to fill after a gap, and only a stop-limit controls the price you get.

steps.name: Set the stop price
steps.text: For a sell stop, enter a stop price below the current price. Keep it outside the stock's normal swings and away from obvious round numbers. Then work out roughly how much you would lose if the order filled at that price, and remember it could fill lower.

steps.name: Set the limit price (stop-limit only)
steps.text: Put the limit price a little below the stop price so the order has room to fill. For example, with made-up numbers, you might use a $45 stop and a $44 limit. A wider gap between the two makes a fill more likely, but it also lowers the worst price you could get.

steps.name: Choose how long the order lasts
steps.text: In the duration or time-in-force setting, choose Day if you want the order to expire at today's close. Choose Good-'til-Canceled (GTC) if you want it to stay active until it fills or you cancel it. Check how long your broker keeps GTC orders open and whether stops work outside regular trading hours.

steps.name: Check the order preview
steps.text: Before you submit, check every field on the preview screen: the side (Sell, not Buy), number of shares, order type, stop price, limit price, duration and any fee shown. A wrong side or share count is an easy mistake to make and can be costly.

steps.name: Keep track of open orders
steps.text: Record the order in a simple log (there's a template later in this guide). Check your broker's Open Orders tab regularly, and again after every trade, stock split or change of plan. Cancel or edit any stop that no longer matches what you own.

sections.heading: What Is a Stop-Loss Order?
paragraphs: A stop-loss order tells your broker to sell a stock automatically, at the market price, once it trades at or below a price you choose. That price is called the stop price. Many order screens label this order 'Stop' or 'Stop market'.

A stop-loss order does nothing until the stop price is reached, and while it waits it's usually held by your broker rather than shown to the market. Once the stock trades at or below the stop price, the order triggers and becomes a regular market order. It then sells at the best price available at that moment. Brokers differ on what counts as reaching the stop: some use the last trade price, while others use the current bid (the highest price a buyer is offering).

Because a triggered stop-loss becomes a market order, the price you get isn't guaranteed. In a fast-moving market, or when the price gaps, the next available price can be well below your stop. The difference between the price you expected and the price you got is called slippage. Every stop order is built on either a market order or a limit order, so if those are new to you, read our market vs limit order guide first.
Stop orders can also be used to buy, but most beginners use them as sell stops on shares they already own. This guide covers sell stops only.
bullets: Trigger: the stop price you set
Turns into: a market order
Puts first: getting out of the position
Main risk: selling well below the stop in a fast market or after an overnight gap

sections.heading: What Is a Stop-Limit Order?
paragraphs: A stop-limit order is a sell order with two prices: a stop price that switches the order on, and a limit price that sets the lowest price you'll accept.

When the stock trades at or below the stop price, a stop-limit order becomes a limit order to sell at your limit price or higher. If no buyer will pay at least the limit price, nothing sells. The order stays open for the duration you chose, and you still own the shares.

How far apart you set the stop and the limit is a trade-off. If the limit equals the stop, a quick drop can skip past both and the order never fills. Setting the limit a little below the stop makes a fill more likely, but it also lowers the worst price you've agreed to accept.

A stop-limit order suits you if avoiding a bad price matters more than getting out at any cost. The catch is that it can fail in a sharp sell-off, which is exactly when you'd most want out. It can also fill only partly, selling some shares at your limit or better and leaving the rest unsold.
bullets: Trigger: the stop price
Turns into: a limit order at your limit price
Puts first: control over the price
Main risk: no sale, or only a partial sale, so you keep holding a falling stock

sections.heading: Stop Loss vs Stop Limit Order for Beginners: A Gap-Down Example
paragraphs: An overnight gap shows the difference between the two orders most clearly. A gap happens when a stock closes at one price and opens much lower the next day, without ever trading at the prices in between.

Here's a made-up example. You own 100 shares of a fictional company, Example Corp, which closes on Tuesday at $50. You've placed a sell stop at $45 because a $5 drop is the most you want to accept. After the market closes, the company reports disappointing results. On Wednesday morning the stock opens at $38.

With a stop-loss order at $45, the stock never traded at $45. It jumped straight from $50 to $38. The first trade at or below your stop is around $38, so your order triggers at the open and becomes a market order. You'd probably sell near $38, or lower if many people are selling. Instead of losing about $5 a share ($500 on 100 shares), you lose about $12 a share (roughly $1,200), before any fees.

With a stop-limit order (stop $45, limit $44), the order also triggers at the open, but it becomes a limit order to sell at $44 or higher. Buyers are paying around $38, so nobody takes your $44 offer and nothing sells. If the stock keeps sliding to $33, you still own all 100 shares. If it climbs back to $44 or higher before the order expires, it might sell then, but that isn't guaranteed.

Both orders did exactly what they were built to do. The stop-loss got you out, and the stop-limit protected your price. The lesson for beginners is that no basic stop order can protect you from a gap. It only decides what happens after the price has already moved.

Gaps don't only happen overnight. Trading halts and sudden crashes during the day can have a similar effect. In the US 'flash crash' of May 2010, for example, some stop orders that had turned into market orders filled at prices far below where the shares had traded minutes earlier.
bullets: Stop-loss after a gap: triggers at the open and sells near the new, lower price
Stop-limit after a gap: triggers, but may not sell if the stock opened below your limit
Neither order type can stop the gap from happening

sections.heading: Trailing Stops in Brief
paragraphs: A trailing stop is a stop order whose stop price follows a rising stock upward, by a set dollar amount or percentage, but never moves down.

Here's an example with made-up numbers. You buy at $50 and set a 10% trailing stop, so the stop starts at $45. If the stock climbs to $60, the stop rises to $54. If the stock then slips to $55, the stop stays at $54. If the stock trades at $54, the order triggers.

Most trailing stops become market orders when triggered, so they carry the same gap risk as a stop-loss: an overnight drop can sell well below the trailing stop price. Some brokers also offer a trailing stop-limit, which adds the stop-limit's risk of not selling at all. Whether trailing stops are available, and exactly how the trail is calculated, depends on your broker.

The hard part is choosing how far the stop trails behind the price. A close trail can be triggered by normal daily ups and downs. A loose trail can give back a large part of a gain before it triggers.
bullets: Trails by: a dollar amount or a percentage
Moves: up with the price, never down (for sell orders)
Carries the same gap risk as a regular stop-loss

sections.heading: Order Duration: Day vs Good-'til-Canceled (GTC)
paragraphs: Order duration, also called time in force, sets how long a stop order stays active. A Day order expires at the end of today's regular trading session. A good-'til-canceled (GTC) order stays active until it fills or you cancel it.

Day orders suit investors who only want protection for one session, such as a volatile day they plan to watch. The downside is that you must place the order again each day for ongoing protection, and that's easy to forget.

GTC orders are convenient because you set them once. However, many brokers limit how long a GTC order can stay open, and some cancel or adjust open orders after events such as stock splits. The bigger risk is human: a GTC stop can sit unnoticed for months and trigger after your plans have changed.

Trading outside normal hours adds another twist. At many brokers, regular stop orders only trigger during the regular session. News released after the close or before the open can't trigger your stop until the market opens, and that's how the gap in the example above happens.
bullets: Day: expires at today's close, so place it again if you still want it
GTC: stays open until it fills, you cancel it, or your broker's time limit runs out
Check: your broker's GTC time limit, what it does with open orders after a stock split, and its rules for trading outside normal hours

sections.heading: Common Stop-Order Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
paragraphs: Three mistakes catch many beginners: setting stops too tight, putting them on obvious round numbers, and forgetting about orders that are still open.

A stop that's too tight sits inside the stock's normal movement, so ordinary wobbles trigger it. Say a stock often moves around 3% in a day and your stop is 2% below the current price (example figures only). A routine dip can sell your shares just before the price recovers, which traders call being 'stopped out'. Before choosing a distance, look at how much the stock usually moves over a few days or weeks.

Round numbers such as $50 or $100 are popular stop levels, so orders can bunch up there. A brief dip to that level may trigger many of them at once, and the burst of selling can push the price lower before it bounces back. Some investors pick less obvious prices for this reason, though no choice of price guarantees a better result.

Forgotten orders cause trouble when a GTC stop outlives its purpose. A stop might trigger months after you decided to hold for the long term, or a stop for 100 shares might still be open after you sold half of them. Depending on your broker and account type, an order that no longer matches your holdings may be rejected or behave in ways you didn't expect.

Other common mistakes include assuming a stop guarantees a maximum loss and setting a stop-limit with no gap between the stop and the limit. Another is using stops on rarely traded stocks. On those stocks the bid-ask spread (the gap between what buyers offer and what sellers ask) is often wide, which can mean poor sale prices.
bullets: Too tight: base the distance on how much the stock usually moves, not a random percentage
Round numbers: obvious prices can attract clusters of stop orders
Forgotten orders: check the Open Orders (or Orders) tab on a regular schedule and after every trade
Rarely traded stocks: check the bid-ask spread and trading volume before relying on a stop

sections.heading: Why Long-Term Index Investors Often Don't Need Stops
paragraphs: Many long-term index investors don't use stop orders. Their strategy depends on staying invested through downturns, and a stop is designed to get you out during one.

A broad index fund holds many companies, so the risk of one company collapsing (a common reason to use a stop) is spread across the whole portfolio. Market-wide falls do happen, and broad markets have historically recovered over long periods. But past performance doesn't guarantee future results, and some recoveries have taken years.

A stop on an index fund can turn a temporary fall into a permanent sale. You then have to decide when to buy back in, and getting two timing decisions right is harder than getting one right. Selling in a taxable account may also mean a tax bill, depending on where you live. Each sale and repurchase can also cost you in fees and bid-ask spreads.

Instead of stops, long-term investors often manage risk in three ways. They choose a mix of stocks, bonds and cash that suits how long they plan to invest (their asset allocation). They keep an emergency fund so they aren't forced to sell in a downturn. And they rebalance from time to time to keep that mix on target. Stops may still make sense for some people, such as someone with a lot of money in a single stock or a short timeframe. That's a personal decision worth discussing with a licensed adviser.
bullets: Index funds already spread out much of the risk of one company failing
Stops can lock in losses during temporary market dips
Selling may trigger taxes and costs, and leaves you deciding when to buy back in
A suitable asset mix, an emergency fund and rebalancing are common alternatives

sections.heading: What to Check With Your Broker (Plus an Order Log Template)
paragraphs: Before you place any stop order, check how your broker handles triggers, fees, order duration and trading outside normal hours, because these rules differ between firms and countries. Most brokers have a help page that explains their order types, and reading it once can save you from an expensive surprise.

A simple order log helps you avoid forgotten GTC stops. Use a notebook, spreadsheet or note-taking app with one line per order and these columns: Date placed | Ticker | Shares | Order type | Stop price | Limit price | Duration | Reason (one sentence) | Next review date. Your broker's Open Orders tab is still the source of truth. The log just reminds you why each order exists and when to look at it again.

Rules, taxes and investor protections differ by country. In the US, the SEC's Investor.gov site explains order types in plain language. Elsewhere, check your local financial regulator. This article is general information, not advice to buy, sell or hold any investment. A licensed financial adviser can help with decisions about your own money.
bullets: What price triggers a stop: the last trade, the current bid, or something else
Whether stops work in pre-market and after-hours trading
How long a GTC order can stay open
What happens to open orders after stock splits, mergers or special dividends
Commissions or fees for each order type
Whether stops are allowed on everything you own (some brokers restrict certain securities)

recommendations.best_for: Investors who want a simple, self-built log of their open stop orders (ticker, stop and limit prices, duration, a one-line reason and a next review date) so GTC orders don't get forgotten. Its pages and databases make the order-log template in this guide easy to set up. Check Notion's site for current plans and features.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who expects it to place, watch or trigger trades. Notion isn't a brokerage or trading tool, so your broker's Open Orders tab is still the source of truth. You don't need it if you only have one or two orders, where a phone note or spreadsheet works just as well, or if you're a long-term index investor who doesn't use stops.

faq.question: Is a stop-loss or a stop-limit order better for beginners?
faq.answer: Neither is always better, because they solve different problems. A stop-loss (stop-market) order puts getting out first and accepts that it may sell below the stop. A stop-limit order puts price first and accepts that it may not sell at all. Many beginners who hold diversified funds for the long term decide they don't need either.

faq.question: Does a stop-loss order guarantee I won't lose more than a set amount?
faq.answer: No. A stop-loss only guarantees that a market order is sent once the stop price is reached. It doesn't guarantee the price you get. If a stock gaps down overnight or falls very fast, it can sell well below your stop, so you can lose more than you planned.

faq.question: Do stop orders trigger in pre-market or after-hours trading?
faq.answer: At many brokers, regular stop orders only work during normal market hours. That's one reason news released overnight can make a stock gap past your stop. Some brokers let certain order types work outside normal hours, so check your broker's rules before relying on a stop around earnings reports or other scheduled news.

faq.question: How far below the current price should I set a stop?
faq.answer: There's no single right distance, and only you (or your adviser) can judge what fits your position. A common approach is to look at how much the stock normally moves and set the stop outside that range, so everyday swings don't trigger it. It also helps to decide how much money you're prepared to lose on the whole position, remembering that a gap can push the loss higher.

faq.question: Do stop orders cost more than regular orders?
faq.answer: That depends on your broker and country. Some brokers charge the same fee for every order type, while others price some order types differently. A triggered stop-loss can also cost you through slippage and the bid-ask spread, so check your broker's current fee schedule.

faq.question: Do stop-loss and stop-limit orders work the same way for crypto?
faq.answer: Many crypto exchanges offer stop-limit orders, and some offer stop-market orders, with the same trade-off. But crypto trades around the clock and can swing very sharply, so slippage, unfilled orders and exchange outages are real risks. Crypto is highly volatile and you can lose everything you put in, scams and rug pulls are common, and coins held on an exchange are at risk if the platform fails, freezes withdrawals or is hacked. Protections usually differ from regulated bank deposits or brokerage accounts, so check your exchange's rules and your local regulator's warnings before relying on any stop.

conclusion: Stop-loss and stop-limit orders give different answers to one question: when the price falls fast, do you want a likely exit, or control over the price you accept? A stop-loss gets you out but doesn't control the price. A stop-limit controls the price but may not get you out. Neither one can stop a gap. If you use stops, set them based on how the stock actually moves, choose how long they last on purpose, keep a simple order log, and check your open orders often. If you're a long-term index investor, ask whether your asset mix and emergency fund already do the job a stop would. For the basics behind all of this, see our market vs limit order guide. Rules, fees and taxes differ by broker and country, so for decisions about your own money, check with your local regulator or a licensed financial adviser.
